title: AI Agents and the Augmentation Agenda
speaker: Arvind Narayanan
content: The dominant paradigm in AI research and development envisions the goal as automation of tasks and entire jobs. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description The dominant paradigm in AI research and development envisions the goal as automation of tasks and entire jobs. But another, comparatively marginalized vision has existed since the beginning of AI — that of augmenting workers and amplifying human potential. In this talk, it is argued that the automation agenda is struggling even on purely commercial grounds, and it is time to invest more into augmentation. Building agents for collaboration instead of automation requires elevating a set of underexplored research challenges in human-computer interaction. Such agents can better serve human flourishing, promote broader economic growth, and put into motion the “pro-worker AI” that economists have advocated for. This talk is based on a collaboration with Gabriel Unger. Bio: Arvind Narayanan is a professor of computer science at Princeton University and the director of the Center for Information Technology Policy. He is a co-author of the book AI Snake Oil and a newsletter of the same name which is read by 60,000 researchers, policy makers, journalists, and AI enthusiasts. He previously co-authored two widely used computer science textbooks: Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Technologies and Fairness in Machine Learning . Narayanan led the Princeton Web Transparency and Accountability Project to uncover how companies collect and use our personal information. His work was among the first to show how machine learning reflects cultural stereotypes. Narayanan was one of TIME’s inaugural list of 100 most influential people in AI. He is a recipient of the Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers (PECASE) This talk will be livestreamed and recorded. The recording will be posted to the CITP website, the CITP YouTube channel and the University Media Central channel. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Traditional hard clustering methods fail to capture the complex, overlapping risk linkages present in modern markets. While recent work (Ding et al., 2024) identifies broad block structures in stock co-jumps, we demonstrate that this framework can be significantly enhanced by incorporating mixed membership. Specifically, we propose a Degree Corrected Mixed Membership network model with Dependent Multivariate Poisson edges that allows stocks to belong to multiple latent risk communities simultaneously and a corresponding estimation algorithm. We prove that our estimator is asymptotically consistent. Empirically, we show that: (1) the mixed membership framework reveals a more informative and granular risk structure than rigid classifications; (2) peer groups defined by our model generate momentum strategies that significantly outperform benchmarks such as selfmomentum, or momentum based on GICS or analyst coverage; and (3) a "purity" measure derived from our model predicts stock volatility and Sharpe ratios, offering a new dimension for risk profiling. Bio: Yingying Li is Fung Term Professor of Business (馮氏商學教授) and Chair Professor at the Department of Information System, Business Statistics and Operations Management (ISOM) and the Department of Finance at Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST). She served as acting head of the FinTech Thrust at HKUST(GZ) at its initial stage. Before joining HKUST, she also held positions as lecturer and postdoctoral fellow at the Bendheim Center for Finance and the Operations Research and Financial Engineering department at Princeton University. Dr. Li received her Ph. D in Statistics from the University of Chicago. Prof. Li's research focuses on statistical learning for financial big data, large portfolio optimization, individualized financial decision making, volatility estimation and prediction etc. Prof. Li has published in top journals in statistics, finance and economics, such as Econometrica , Review of Financial Studies , Journal of Financial Economics , Annals of Statistics , Journal of American Statistical Association , and Journal of Econometrics . Prof. Li is an RGC Senior Research Fellow, elected Fellow of the Society for Financial Econometrics (SoFiE), Fellow of Journal of Econometrics, NSFC YSF Cat-A awardee, and NSFC Excellent Young Scientist. She served or is serving as an Associate Editor for the Journal of American Statistical Association , Management Science , Journal of Econometrics , Journal of Business & Economic Statistics and Journal of Financial Econometrics ; a council member for the Society for Financial Econometrics, and a panel member of the Hong Kong Research Grants Council (RGC) and the University Grants Committee (UGC). https://yyli.finstar.hk/bio Event Category S. speaker: Xihong Lin, Harvard University
content: Abstract: Large-scale causal mediation, replication, and pleiotropy analyses may appear to be unrelated problems. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Large-scale causal mediation, replication, and pleiotropy analyses may appear to be unrelated problems. However, they all involve testing a large number of composite null hypotheses, a statistically challenging task arising in many scientific settings, especially in genomic and biobank studies. A composite null is defined as the union of K individual null hypotheses, and is rejected only when all individual hypotheses are false. We will first show that classical tests such as Wald and likelihood ratios fail to follow chi-square tests and are often overly conservative, leading to substantial power loss. We propose several approaches to address this problem. We show that the divide-aggregate composite-null test (DACT) by leveraging a large number of tests and Efron’s empirical null framework works well when signals are weak and sparse, but can exhibit error rate inflation in the presence of dense and strong signals. To overcome this limitation, we propose a tail likelihood ratio (TLR) test that is robust and powerful across diverse settings, encompassing weak to strong signal strengths, sparse to dense signal proportions, symmetric and unsymmetric signal distributions, and correlations among the large number of tests. We show that local FDR for a large number of composite nulls can be expressed as a function of a likelihood ratio, which is approximated in the tail region to construct the TLR statistic. We derive the null distribution of the TLR statistic by leveraging information from the large number of tests, and account for correlation among tests using a principal component-based approximation. Extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed method maintains accurate error rate control in multiple comparisons and exhibits superior power gains compared to existing methods. Applications to multiple examples further illustrate the performance and utility of the proposed framework.

title: The Bystander Privacy Problem
speaker: Helen Nissenbaum
content: Not first to pose a threat to “bystander privacy,” Meta Ray-bans (and similar), have drawn public ire, even disgust. Despite this, we have yet to see decisive pushback from regulatory bodies, and the companies rolling out these products, without a trace of irony, swear to an ongoing commitment to privacy. Setting aside corporate self-dealing and misdirection, Nissenbaum is interested, particularly, in the role of conceptual failure in sustaining the status quo. She explains why a privacy framework that has shaped regulatory thinking and institutional practice for decades (despite
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Not first to pose a threat to “bystander privacy,” Meta Ray-bans (and similar), have drawn public ire, even disgust. Despite this, we have yet to see decisive pushback from regulatory bodies, and the companies rolling out these products, without a trace of irony, swear to an ongoing commitment to privacy. Setting aside corporate self-dealing and misdirection, Nissenbaum is interested, particularly, in the role of conceptual failure in sustaining the status quo. She explains why a privacy framework that has shaped regulatory thinking and institutional practice for decades (despite overwhelming counterevidence) bears significant responsibility for this stalemate. Offering the lens of contextual integrity as an alternative, she argues (spoiler alert) that singling out bystanders for special treatment, in fact, promulgates dominant truisms that we’d be better off without. Bio: Helen Nissenbaum is the Andrew H. and Ann R. Tisch Professor of information science at Cornell Tech and the Cornell Ann S. Bowers College of Computing and Information Science. She is also the director of the Digital Life Initiative , which was launched in 2017 at Cornell Tech to explore societal perspectives surrounding the development and application of digital technology, focusing on ethics, policy, politics, and quality of life. Nissenbaum’s research takes an ethical perspective on policy, law, science, and engineering related to information technology, computing, digital media, and data science. Topics have included privacy, trust, accountability, security, and values in technology design. Her books include “Obfuscation: A User’s Guide for Privacy and Protest” with Finn Brunton and “Privacy in Context: Technology, Policy, and the Integrity of Social Life.” Grants from the NSF , AFOSR , and the U.S. DHHS-ONC have supported her work. She was a recipient of the 2014 Barwise Prize of the American Philosophical Association and an honorary doctorate from Leuphana University, Germany. Nissenbaum has contributed to the development of privacy-enhancing software, including TrackMeNot and AdNauseam. Nissenbaum holds a Ph.D. in philosophy from Stanford University and a B.A. in philosophy and mathematics from the University of the Witwatersrand, South Africa. Motivation for solving such problems arises in modern “distribution free” statistical learning problems. We will highlight some of the challenges of solving such problems, including that subgradients of stochastic convex functions do not converge uniformly, and also demonstrate some new geometric tools to show that solving the problem is in fact possible. Bio: John Duchi is an associate professor of Statistics and Electrical Engineering at Stanford University. His work spans statistical learning, optimization, information theory, and computation, with a few driving goals. (1) To discover statistical learning procedures that optimally trade between real-world resources — computation, communication, privacy provided to study participants — while maintaining statistical efficiency. (2) To build efficient large-scale optimization methods that address the spectrum of optimization, machine learning, and data analysis problems we face, allowing us to move beyond bespoke solutions to methods that robustly work. (3) To develop tools to assess and guarantee the validity of — and confidence we should have in — machine-learned systems. Event Category Optimization Seminar ORFE Department Colloquia

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: We study a system of interacting diffusions with heterogeneous pairwise interactions, so the particle system is non-exchangeable. In the first part of the talk, we develop a quantitative, non-asymptotic approach to mean field approximation by comparing the law of any subcollection of particles with a suitably chosen product measure and proving sharp relative entropy bounds. The proof uses a BBGKY hierarchy adapted to the non-exchangeable setting and an unexpected connection with first-passage percolation. In the second part, we establish a universal central limit theorem for the global fluctuation field around the McKean-Vlasov limit. Under suitable structural and denseness conditions on the interaction matrix, the fluctuations converge to the same Gaussian SPDE as in the classical exchangeable mean field case. For $m_n$-regular graphs, this holds when $m_n/\sqrt n\to\infty$, and a spatial interaction model shows that the $n^{-1/2}$ denseness threshold is sharp. The proof builds on the sharp propagation of chaos estimates developed in the first part, together with functional inequalities and an analysis in negative Sobolev spaces. Based on joint work with Daniel Lacker and Fuzhong Zhou, and on joint work with Mykhaylo Shkolnikov. Short Bio : Lane Chun Yeung is a postdoctoral research associate at Carnegie Mellon University, mentored by Mykhaylo Shkolnikov. He received his Ph.D. in Operations Research from Columbia University, where he was advised by Daniel Lacker and Ioannis Karatzas. His research interests include interacting particle systems, mean field models, mathematical finance, and stochastic control and games. Event Category Stochastic Analysis and Financial Mathematics Seminar

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Min-norm interpolators naturally arise as implicitly regularized limits of modern neural networks and other widely used algorithms. While their out-of-distribution risk has recently been analyzed in settings where test samples are unavailable during training, many practical applications allow partial access to target data. The behavior of min-norm interpolation in such settings remains poorly understood. In this talk, I will present a sharp characterization of the risk of min-norm interpolators under both covariate and model shifts. Our results yield several important insights. For instance, in the presence of model shift, incorporating additional data can actually harm prediction performance when the signal-to-noise ratio is low. Conversely, for higher signal-to-noise ratios, transfer learning is beneficial, provided the shift-to-signal ratio remains below a precise threshold, which I will define. To reach these conclusions, we develop novel anisotropic local laws, representing new advances in random matrix theory for heterogeneous data problems. I will also discuss applications of our results to the challenge of combining real data with synthetic data generated by AI models. This talk is based on joint works with Anvit Garg, Kenny Gu, Yanke Song, Debarghya Mukherjee, and Pragya Sur. Bio: Sohom Bhattacharya is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Statistics at the University of Florida. Before joining UF, he was a Postdoctoral Research Associate in the Department of Operations Research and Financial Engineering at Princeton University. He received his Ph.D. in Statistics from Stanford University in 2022. His research interests lie at the intersection of high-dimensional statistics and statistical machine learning. He has also worked in applied probability, focusing on random graphs and inference in networks. Event Category S. S. Wilks Memorial Seminar in Statistics

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description The Accelerator has acquired several years of Comscore panel data capturing real-world mobile and desktop browsing behavior, enriched with detailed demographic information. This dataset provides session-level insights into how people use their devices — what apps they open, what websites they visit, how long they spend, and in what sequence. Unlike social media APIs or traditional surveys, these data capture the invisible majority of online behavior: browsing, reading, and app usage that leaves no public trace. This talk will open with an overview on the data from Professor Jacob Shapiro, followed by two use cases from Kevin Greene at the Empirical Studies of Conflict Project and Alejandro Cuevas from CITP. The Accelerator Comscore dataset is available for Princeton-based research projects and is currently being used across 10+ projects spanning a variety of subject matter. Speakers: Alejandro Cuevas is a researcher focused on the shady, suspicious, and illicit corners of the Internet––and how emerging technologies like generative AI both influence and are influenced by these spaces. He blends gonzo and computational social science: first-person fieldwork in underground communities paired with large-scale measurements. His work on darkweb marketplaces has informed criminal investigations and the development of law enforcement tools. More recently, he’s explored how generative AI is reshaping the online information ecosystem, including how people build audiences and craft political narratives––the latter as a research consultant at Microsoft Research. He earned his Ph.D. in societal computing from Carnegie Mellon University in 2025, where he was advised by Nicolas Christin and honored with a CyLab Presidential Fellowship. He holds a B.S. with honors from Penn State. Outside academia, he co-founded Redoux, a NYC-based fragrance brand. Kevin Greene is an academic research manager in the Empirical Studies of Conflict Project at Princeton University leading the Digital Conflict and Information Integrity project. He was previously a postdoctoral fellow in the Computer Science Department at Dartmouth College. He holds a Ph.D. in Political Science from the University of Pittsburgh. His research examines the role of information and information communication technologies in international and domestic politics. Ongoing projects investigate the spread of unreliable content from algorithmic recommendations, the social and political risks posed by generative AI, and the strategies employed by foreign influence operations. His research has been funded by the National Science Foundation, Lockheed Martin Advanced Technology Labs, and Microsoft and published in Science Advances , PNAS Nexus , the American Political Science Review , Political Analysis , the Journal of Politics , and Political Communication among others. Manoel Horta Ribeiro is an assistant professor at Princeton University in the Department of Computer Science and affiliated with CITP. He received his doctoral degree in Switzerland at EPFL’s Data Science Lab, working with Bob West, and his MSc and BSc in Brazil at UFMG. Ribeiro works at the intersection of computational social science, artificial intelligence, and social computing. He likes doing research that tackles real-world issues and provides actionable insights. Ideally, these insights translate into policy and design changes. Ribeiro's work has also received extensive media coverage, helping shape the public debate around online platforms and generative AI. Jacob N. Shapiro is a professor of politics and international affairs and directs the Empirical Studies of Conflict Project and the Accelerator Initiative. His research on conflict, economic development, security, and technology leverages a wide range of data from administrative records of combat events, to satellite imagery, to social media data and browser telemetry. Shapiro received the 2016 Karl Deutsch Award from ISA, given to a scholar younger than 40 or within 10 years of earning a Ph.D. who has made the most significant contribution to the study of international relations. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: We study systems of reflected Brownian motions on the half-line in which each particle is pulled toward the origin by the local times at zero of all the particles. When the interaction is too strong, the system breaks down in finite time. We characterize the breakdown completely through a dynamic graph structure, construct the mean-field limit, and describe how the system continues past breakdown as a solution of the extended Skorokhod problem. At criticality, the finite system survives for a time of order N while its mean-field limit survives forever; we explain this metastability through an exact skew-product decomposition. Bio: Graeme Baker is a Term Assistant Professor in the Department of Statistics at Columbia University, where he also teaches in the M.A. in Mathematical Finance program. He received his PhD in Applied and Computational Mathematics from Princeton University, advised by Mykhaylo Shkolnikov. His research concerns interacting particle systems with singular interactions, probabilistic solutions of free boundary problems, and the calibration of stochastic models to financial data. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: We study distributional transportability of treatment effects in a “cross-site, one-armed target” design, where both treated and control units are observed in a source site, but only control units are observed in a target site. Our object of interest is not estimating the average treatment effect, but recovering the full treated distribution in the target site using transfer knowledge from the source site, while allowing cross-site heterogeneity in measurement systems, observed features, outcome reporting, population composition, and latent contextual factors. We model cross-site heterogeneity through a transformation between the sites that transports the joint feature-outcome distributions. This transformation is learned from comparing the observed control samples in the source and target sites, using an optimal transport criterion. The learned transformation is then applied to the source treated sample to construct a synthetic sample from the target treated distribution. We establish consistency of the learned transformation and convergence of the resulting synthetic empirical distribution to the target treated distribution. Simulation studies across multiple data-generating scenarios and a real-world application to patient-derived xenograft (PDX) data demonstrate that our framework recovers the full distributional properties of the target treated population. title: Towards Globally Equitable AI
speaker: Aditya Vashistha
content: AI has the power to drive meaningful change, but its benefits have remained concentrated among privileged communities in the West, which account for only a small fraction of the global population. Even conversations about AI risks are rooted in Western contexts, despite AI’s widespread use across the world. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description AI has the power to drive meaningful change, but its benefits have remained concentrated among privileged communities in the West, which account for only a small fraction of the global population. Even conversations about AI risks are rooted in Western contexts, despite AI’s widespread use across the world. Consequently, current AI technologies not only lack representation of diverse non-Western cultures and languages, but also perpetuate harmful stereotypes about people in these cultures. This talk will examine these challenges through case studies of my work with people with disabilities, women, and emerging users of AI-based technologies in the Global South. Both the promises and pitfalls of existing AI systems will be highlighted, illustrating how they often fail those who are most marginalized. By centering these overlooked perspectives, we will discuss pathways for designing AI technologies that are more inclusive, representative, and equitable on a global scale. Bio: Aditya Vashistha is an assistant professor of Computing and Information Science at Cornell University, where he directs the Cornell Global AI Initiative, an interdisciplinary, university-wide effort to integrate global perspectives into the design, development, evaluation, and governance of AI. His research builds and studies AI technologies that advance equity and improve socioeconomic outcomes for marginalized communities. His work has led to widely used systems impacting over 300,000 people in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa, earning multiple best paper awards. His work has been recognized with prestigious accolades, including the Facebook Access Innovation Prize, the UW College of Engineering Award, the Meta Fellowship, Google Faculty Award, Microsoft Faculty Award, and the President’s and Provost’s Faculty Award for Excellence in Research, Teaching, and Service at Cornell. He holds a Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of Washington, where his dissertation received the William Chan Memorial Dissertation Award and the WAGS/ProQuest Innovation in Technology Award. speaker: Liat Krawczyk

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Artificial intelligence is advancing faster than the institutions, workforces, and systems expected to absorb it. The challenge ahead is therefore not only one of technological innovation, but of deployment: how do we translate rapidly evolving capabilities into broad-based economic opportunity, institutional capacity, and public benefit? This talk will explore the New Jersey AI Hub as an emerging model for tackling that challenge. A public-private initiative founded by Princeton University, the State of New Jersey, Microsoft, and CoreWeave, the Hub brings together universities, government, industry, startups, and communities to accelerate AI innovation and adoption. Liat Krawczyk will discuss the Hub’s work across entrepreneurship, workforce development, applied AI, and responsible governance—and the larger question underlying it: what new forms of collaboration and infrastructure are needed when technological change moves faster than any one institution can respond? Bio: Liat Krawczyk is the inaugural executive director of the New Jersey AI Hub, a public-private initiative launched by Princeton University, the State of New Jersey, Microsoft, and CoreWeave to advance AI innovation, adoption, and workforce development. Previously, she served at the U.S. Department of Commerce’s CHIPS Program Office, where she led workforce strategy and child care efforts tied to the nation’s historic investment in semiconductor manufacturing. Earlier, she led innovation initiatives at the New York City Economic Development Corporation, including work spanning cybersecurity, emerging technology, and the care economy, and has built and advised organizations at the intersection of technology, economic development, and public policy. Her work focuses on a central question of technological change: how institutions, industries, and communities can adapt quickly enough to turn innovation into broadly shared economic opportunity. This talk will be livestreamed and recorded. The recording will be posted to the CITP website, the CITP YouTube channel and the University Media Central channel. title: From Code to Care: The Moralization of Healthcare Machine Learning
speaker: Shira Zilberstein
content: Artificial intelligence is widely promoted as a promising solution to healthcare challenges, yet its clinical benefits still remain uncertain and its risks persistent. Drawing on extensive fieldwork with researchers developing machine-learning applications for healthcare, this talk demonstrates how practitioners sustain AI’s legitimacy by framing their work as serving the common good. It is argued that “moralization”—the work of aligning technological projects with values such as equity, care, and wellbeing—generates consensus and momentum for technological solutions to social problems amid
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Artificial intelligence is widely promoted as a promising solution to healthcare challenges, yet its clinical benefits still remain uncertain and its risks persistent. Drawing on extensive fieldwork with researchers developing machine-learning applications for healthcare, this talk demonstrates how practitioners sustain AI’s legitimacy by framing their work as serving the common good. It is argued that “moralization”—the work of aligning technological projects with values such as equity, care, and wellbeing—generates consensus and momentum for technological solutions to social problems amid uncertainty. At the same time, the moralization of machine learning risks obscuring technical limitations, diffusing accountability, and diverting attention from alternative approaches. Using healthcare AI to illuminate broader transformations in scientific authority as knowledge production becomes increasingly applied, interdisciplinary, and problem-oriented, it is shown how technical authority is established not through claims of neutrality or detachment, but by building relationships across institutional and professional boundaries. Bio: Shira Zilberstein is a sociologist whose research investigates the moral and organizational foundations of knowledge production, with particular attention to how science and technology are used to define and address social problems. Her current work focuses on the development and governance of AI models for healthcare. Using qualitative methods, she studies how researchers and practitioners justify and seek to ensure the social value of their work. She is especially interested in how research communities navigate uncertainty and sustain commitments to technological innovation even in the face of contested outcomes and limitations. Shira holds a Ph.D. in sociology from Harvard University, where she was a Science and Technology Studies Fellow and a BA in sociology and history from Northwestern University. Her research has been supported by the National Science Foundation, the American Sociological Association, the Russell Sage Foundation, and the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, among others. She has collaborated with researchers at MIT, Duke, and Yale on projects related to the development and governance of healthcare AI. At Princeton, she is also affiliated with the Princeton Societal AI Initiative. This talk will not be livestreamed or recorded. rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Talk information: TBA Bio: Alia ElKattan is a researcher who examines the sociopolitical implications of online platforms and emerging technologies. She obtained her Ph.D. at NYU Politics, where her research focused on how the design of technology mediates the acquisition of political information, and how to motivate and safeguard responsible, healthy, and critical engagement with emerging technologies such as large language models and conversational agents. She also has a creative technology practice which leverages play and interactive storytelling to both demystify opaque technologies, and expand public imaginaries of alternative technological futures. ElKattan is a grantee of the Responsible Technology Youth Power Fund and a two-time winner of Mozilla Foundation’s Creative Media Award for work on AI bias, data transparency, user choice in algorithmic feeds. Her work has been published in venues such as Sociological Science, FAccT, the Journal for Quantitative Description, and and been presented in media festivals including the International Documentary Festival Amsterdam (IDFA) in the Netherlands, Sheffield DocFest in the UK, and March On Festival in Washington, DC, among others. When not writing code or papers, ElKattan can most often be found playing football (soccer), skateboarding, or making playlists.
